questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Several routes to the same visible outcome
questions.learningObjective: Recognise that one outcome can be reached by several routes
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that one source sentence was rendered as a single flowing line, while an earlier draft split the same idea into three short clauses. What does this show about the visible outcome of a translation?

options.text: The shorter version is more accurate, because shorter renderings preserve more of the original meaning.
options.misconception: judges accuracy by length instead of by what the source says

options.text: The same meaning can be reached by more than one arrangement of words, so the outcome alone does not identify the route.
The split version is the better translation, since the source itself uses long sentences throughout.
options.misconception: judges a rendering by the sentence length of the whole source

options.text: The difference proves the two drafts were made from different source texts, rather than from the same one.
options.misconception: infers a different source text from a difference in arrangement

questions.explanation: One meaning can be reached by several arrangements of words, so the finished line cannot show how the translator got there. Fluency is a property of the outcome, and it does not identify the route that produced it.
questions.hint: Ask what the finished line cannot reveal about the route.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The scope condition as part of a finding
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the scope of a finding must be stated with it
questions.stem: A translator's note records that the term the source uses for a regional office was left untranslated throughout the whole volume. Explain why the scope condition belongs inside the finding.

answer.exemplar: The finding is that the regional office was kept in the source language across the whole volume, and that scope is part of the finding rather than a note attached to it. Without the scope, a reader would take the term as a translator's habit in general, when the notes show it was a decision taken throughout this one work, in a book whose other terms were all translated. Recording the scope is what makes the observation about this volume and not about the translator or the language pair.

questions.explanation: The scope says which cases the observation covers, so it belongs inside the finding. Without it, a reader would take a decision taken throughout this one volume as a general habit of the translator.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would wrongly conclude without it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Applying a finding where its condition is not met
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a finding may not apply where its condition fails

stimulus.body: A translator's notes on a manual state that footnotes in the source appear only where a term is first defined. The next section of the notes covers a different manual, in which the publisher uses footnotes at the bottom of every page for page references. The translator has proposed applying the first rule to the second manual.

questions.stem: Given this note, what is the strongest objection to applying the first manual's rule to the second manual?

options.text: The two manuals were written by different publishers, so any rule from the first is void for the second.
options.misconception: rejects a rule because the publisher differs, not the condition

options.text: The second manual is shorter, so a rule drawn from a longer work cannot be transferred to it.
options.misconception: refuses a transfer because of length rather than of conditions

options.text: The rule was observed in a source with a different footnote practice, so its condition does not hold in the second manual.
The translator should simply keep the first rule, since one consistent choice is easier to maintain across a whole project.
options.misconception: prefers a consistent house style over the conditions behind a rule

questions.explanation: The rule was observed in a source with a different footnote practice, so the condition behind it is not met in the second manual. A finding carries its conditions, and they must hold where it is applied.
questions.hint: Check the condition under which the rule was observed.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why an order of events does not identify a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: State what an ordered list of events establishes
questions.stem: A translator's notes record three events in order: a chapter was retranslated, a proof was returned, and a printer's slot was booked. What can this sequence of notes establish?

options.text: That the retranslation caused the printer's slot to be booked, since the booking came last in the sequence.
options.misconception: reads the last event in a dated list as the effect of the first

options.text: That the printer's delay caused the retranslation, since proofing often follows a printer's decision.
options.misconception: assumes a standard production order instead of reading the notes

options.text: That the three steps form the standard production sequence the publisher always follows for this title.
options.misconception: assumes a single sequence is the rule the publisher always follows

options.text: That the three events happened in that order, while what connected them is not established by the notes.

questions.explanation: A dated list of events fixes their order and nothing more, and three entries in sequence cannot show what connected them. The notes may be consistent with the usual production order, but they do not claim it.
questions.hint: Ask what the list of events can and cannot fix.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A feedback loop that a linear account cannot order
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a feedback loop that cannot be linearly ordered
questions.stem: In a translator's notes, readers' complaints about a clumsy rendering lead to a revision, and the revised wording pushes other readers toward the same complaint. How should the translator handle this?

options.text: Treat it as a loop, since each step feeds the next and no first step can be identified from the notes alone.
Order it linearly, since the complaint must have come before the revision that answered it.
options.misconception: insists any account must be broken into a straight order

options.text: Record only the revision, since the complaint is an outside reaction rather than part of the process.
options.misconception: treats the feedback as external noise rather than a link

options.text: Report it as two separate cases, since a complaint and a revision cannot belong to one account.
options.misconception: splits a self-sustaining account into disconnected pieces

questions.explanation: When each step produces the next, the notes describe a loop, and a linear account must invent a starting point the record does not supply. Naming the loop keeps the mechanism intact.
questions.hint: Ask which direction the arrows actually run.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Recognising and testing a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Identify what locating a threshold requires
questions.stem: A translator's notes observe that source sentences over a certain length were broken into two, while shorter ones were left whole. What would be needed to pin down the threshold?

options.text: A count of how many long sentences the translator rejected outright without reading them at all.
options.misconception: looks for discarded material rather than for cases near the boundary

options.text: Cases that fall just either side of the length in question, so the behaviour can be checked on both sides.
The translator's stated preference for short sentences, which settles the question without any further evidence.
options.misconception: accepts a stated preference in place of checking behaviour

options.text: A second translator's work on the same text, so the threshold can be averaged over two people's habits.
options.misconception: averages two people's habits rather than locating the threshold

questions.explanation: A threshold is a boundary, and it can only be located by testing cases on either side of it. Preference, discarded material and a second translator's habits all tell the translator something else.
questions.hint: Look for cases that sit just above and just below.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Telling a necessary condition from a sufficient one
questions.learningObjective: Tell a necessary condition from a sufficient one
questions.stem: A translator's note says that every rendering the client rejected had been checked by a second reader, and that many checked renderings were accepted. Explain what this note establishes.

answer.exemplar: The note establishes that second reading is necessary for a rendering to be rejected, in the sense that the rejected renderings were among those that had been checked, while many renderings that had been checked were accepted, so checking on its own does not bring about rejection. That makes it a necessary condition within this project rather than a sufficient one. The note does not establish that a second reading would have caught anything in particular, nor that the checking was carried out in the same way in every case, and those are the limits a careful reader should keep in mind.

questions.explanation: All rejected renderings were checked while many checked renderings were accepted, so checking is necessary but not sufficient to cause rejection. A necessary condition must be present for the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask what happens when the condition holds but nothing follows.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A condition present in every success and sufficient for none
questions.learningObjective: Identify a condition that accompanies every success but produces none

stimulus.body: A translator's notes list ten renderings the editor accepted without changes. Every one of them was delivered on time. The same notes also list six renderings delivered late, and four of those were accepted without changes as well. A separate line records that the client always asked for the delivery date to be confirmed in writing.

questions.stem: Given these notes, which statement about the delivery condition is best supported?

options.text: Delivering on time is sufficient for acceptance, because every on-time rendering was accepted without changes.
options.misconception: mistakes a condition present in every success for one that produces it

options.text: Delivering on time has no bearing on acceptance, because the notes record acceptance decisions rather than causes.
options.misconception: dismisses a condition because the notes were written to record decisions

options.text: Delivering on time appears in every acceptance but in no case guarantees one, so it is not sufficient on its own.
The client only ever accepts late work, since four late renderings were accepted without changes.
options.misconception: reads a few late acceptances as a settled client preference

questions.explanation: Every acceptance came with an on-time delivery, yet some late deliveries were accepted too. So the condition appears in every success without producing any of them, which is what makes it insufficient.
questions.hint: Check whether the condition ever arrives without the outcome.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Several routes to the same visible outcome
questions.learningObjective: Show that one result can be produced by different routes
questions.stem: Two different renderings of the same source line both reached a proof stage, one by tightening the syntax and one by adding a clarifying clause. What does this show about the outcome?

options.text: That the clarifying clause is the better route, since a longer rendering carries more meaning across.
options.misconception: judges a route by the length of the text it produced

options.text: That tightening the syntax is the only route that works, since only it kept the line's length down.
options.misconception: claims exclusivity for one route from a single success

options.text: That both renderings reached the proof stage by accident, since neither matches the source exactly.
options.misconception: treats any departure from the source wording as accidental

options.text: That the same visible result can be reached by different routes, so the result does not reveal which was used.

questions.explanation: The two renderings reached the same point by different arrangements, so the outcome does not identify the route. Judging by length, or claiming one route was the only possible one, misuses the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask what two routes to one result would show.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The scope condition as part of a finding
questions.learningObjective: Record the boundary of a practice found inside one work
questions.stem: A translator's note says the term for the city council was translated in the body of the work but left as an abbreviation in the appendices. What should the translator record about the scope of this practice?

options.text: That it holds in the body only, and that the appendices are excluded, so the finding is not a general rule of the work.
That the practice varies within the work, so no finding about the term can be made at all.
options.misconception: reads a bounded practice as the absence of any finding

options.text: That the abbreviation in the appendices is an error, since consistency is the goal of a translation.
options.misconception: treats variation inside a work as an error to be corrected

options.text: That the note applies to all future translations of the same work, since the practice is now fixed.
options.misconception: extends a note about one work into a rule for future work

questions.explanation: The scope is the body with the appendices excluded, and the finding must carry that boundary. Variation within a work does not cancel a finding about it, and the note says nothing about future work.
questions.hint: Name the part of the work the practice covers.

questions.topic: Applying a finding where its condition is not met
questions.learningObjective: State the condition under which a local observation supports a general rule
questions.stem: A translator's notes report that a term was left untranslated in every dialogue in one chapter. What is the condition that must hold for that note to support a rule about the whole book?

options.text: The other chapters must be translated too, so that the reader can see the term handled differently elsewhere.
options.misconception: requires more translation work instead of a condition on the finding

options.text: The chapter must be typical of how the book handles dialogue, so the observation is not confined to one setting.
The translator must have consulted the client, so that the practice is known to have been deliberate.
options.misconception: treats the translator's intention as the condition of the finding

options.text: The untranslated term must appear at least ten times, so that the observation rests on a large number of cases.
options.misconception: thinks a count of instances is what a general rule requires

questions.explanation: A note about one chapter supports a rule about the book only if the chapter is typical of the book's practice, and the notes are where to say so. Consulting the client speaks to intention, not scope.
questions.hint: Ask whether the chapter is representative of the whole.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why an order of events does not identify a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a dated sequence does not identify a mechanism
questions.stem: A translator's notes record a query being sent, an answer arriving, a change being made, and a proof being sent back. Explain why this sequence does not identify a mechanism.

answer.exemplar: The sequence fixes four things in time: a query, an answer, a change and a returning proof. What produced what is a separate question, and the sequence is silent on it, because the notes record the order of the translator's paperwork rather than any link between the items. The answer may well have caused the change, and the change may well have caused the proof, but a list of dated entries cannot distinguish those links from coincidence, and reading the mechanism into the order is an addition the reader is making rather than something the notes supply.

questions.explanation: The sequence fixes the order of the translator's paperwork and not what produced what. The answer may have caused the change, but dated entries cannot tell a link from a coincidence.
questions.hint: Ask what the dated entries record besides the order.

questions.topic: A feedback loop that a linear account cannot order
questions.learningObjective: Read a self-feeding account as a feedback loop

stimulus.body: A translator's notes record that a glossary was extended after two reviewers complained about a term, and that the extended glossary was then cited by the reviewers as the reason to ask for a third change. The notes also record that the same two reviewers had asked for the third change in an earlier project without the glossary existing.

questions.stem: Given these notes, which reading best fits the account they record?

options.text: A linear sequence, since the complaints came first and the later changes could only follow from them.
options.misconception: forces a straight order on an account with no starting point

options.text: A single decision, since the glossary was extended once and everything afterwards followed from that decision.
options.misconception: treats one decision as the single cause of every later change

options.text: A feedback loop, since each response supplied the reason for the next request and the notes cannot fix a first step.
Two unrelated episodes, since a glossary and a review request cannot belong to one account at all.
options.misconception: splits a self-feeding account into pieces to keep it tidy

questions.explanation: Each response supplies the reason for the next request, and earlier changes were asked for without the glossary, so no step can be named first. A linear account would invent the starting point.
questions.hint: Look for where each step supplies the reason for the next.

questions.learningObjective: Judge how precisely a note locates a threshold
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that italic type was used for emphasis only in sections under a page in length. Which statement about this note is best supported?

options.text: The page length caused the italic type, since the shorter sections are the ones that were emphasised.
options.misconception: confuses a recorded correlation with a demonstrated cause

options.text: Emphasis was used only in short sections, so the threshold is the length of the section.
options.misconception: treats a loose boundary as an exact numerical limit

options.text: The threshold is exactly one page, because the notes describe the change at the page boundary.
options.misconception: fixes a precise threshold that the notes never state

options.text: The notes establish a boundary of some kind, but they do not fix where the boundary falls.

questions.explanation: The notes record a change across a boundary, but not the length of the longest emphasised section, so the boundary cannot be placed. A precise limit is an addition the note does not make.
questions.hint: Ask what the notes would need to say to place the boundary.

options.misconception: turns a necessary condition into a rule for future projects

options.misconception: mistakes a condition present in every praise for one that produces it

options.text: It is present in every praise but produces no praise on its own, so it is insufficient by itself.
It is irrelevant, because the notes record reactions rather than any condition attached to them.
options.misconception: dismisses a condition because the notes were written to record reactions

options.text: It is necessary for praise and sufficient for it as well, because no praised rendering escaped the check.
options.misconception: asserts sufficiency from a claim that only necessity was ever shown

questions.explanation: Every praised rendering was checked but some unchecked ones were praised too, so the check accompanies the praise without producing it. Such a condition is insufficient, though it may be worth recording.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Several routes to the same visible outcome
questions.learningObjective: State what a pair of accepted renderings establishes
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that the same awkward source passage was handled in two ways in two different translations, and both renderings were accepted. Explain what this pair of renderings can and cannot show.

answer.exemplar: The two renderings show that one source passage can be rendered acceptably along more than one route, which is useful to know when a new rendering is required and the earlier one cannot be copied. They do not show that the two routes are equivalent in every respect, because the clients were different and the contexts differed, and they cannot show which route is better, since acceptance by two different clients is not a comparison on one scale. The notes therefore support the plural of the possible routes and nothing about their ranking.

questions.explanation: The two accepted renderings show that one passage can be handled acceptably by more than one route. They cannot show which route is better, since the clients and contexts differ and acceptance is not one scale.
questions.hint: Ask whether acceptance by two clients ranks the routes.

questions.explanation: The notes support a claim about the first edition and a different one about the second, each bounded by its own edition. The same translator across both does not make the finding a property of the work.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Recognising and testing a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Say what evidence would fix a boundary a note only reports
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that quotations were kept in italics up to a certain length and rewritten in the running text beyond it. Explain what the notes would need in order to fix that boundary.

answer.exemplar: The notes would need the length of the longest quotation that was left in italics and the length of the shortest one that was rewritten, or some equivalent observation that brackets the change of practice. As they stand, the note says a boundary exists but does not place it, so a translator consulting these notes could not tell whether a particular quotation would have been kept or rewritten. Adding the two bracketing observations would turn a claim that a threshold exists into a claim about where it lies, which is the difference between a rule that can be applied and one that can only be reported.

questions.explanation: The notes need the longest quotation kept in italics and the shortest rewritten, to bracket the change. As they stand they say a boundary exists without placing it, so no one could apply the rule.
questions.hint: Ask for the two observations that would bracket the change.

That the later revision was an improvement, since a later proof normally improves on an earlier one.
options.misconception: treats recency of a version as evidence that it is the better one

questions.explanation: Two renderings of the line reaching print shows more than one was acceptable, and the notes record no basis for ranking them. Recency, printing and revision do not show which one a reader preferred.

questions.topic: Applying a finding where its condition is not met

questions.stem: A translator's notes record that a client's house style required a space before a colon in dialogue, and a colleague proposes the same rule for a new documentary. Explain the condition problem with that proposal.

answer.exemplar: The rule was recorded for one client's house style, so the condition it rests on is that this client applies that style to this kind of material. A documentary prepared for a different commissioning editor under a different style guide may not have that condition at all, and a rule carried across without checking it would be a rule applied outside its scope. The notes do not tell the colleague what the documentary requires, and the sensible move is to find the commissioning editor's own style rather than to assume the earlier client's practice transfers.

questions.explanation: The rule rests on one client's house style, and a new documentary prepared for someone else may not share that condition. Carrying it across unchecked would apply it outside its scope.
questions.hint: Ask whose style the original rule was recorded for.

questions.stem: Given these notes, which description of the query episode is best supported?

options.text: The editor's reply caused the change and the approval, because the reply is the only recorded link between them.
options.misconception: fills a missing reply with a mechanism it never recorded

options.text: The sequence shows the query was unnecessary, since the proof was approved without any change being made.
options.misconception: reads an unrelated approval as a verdict on the query

options.text: The sequence fixes the order of four events but leaves the replies and their effect on the change unrecorded.
The sequence proves the editor's replies are always acted on, since every reply in the notes was followed by a change.
options.misconception: generalises from a single episode to a rule about all replies

questions.explanation: The notes fix the order of the entries and nothing more, because the reply and its effect are unrecorded. An unrelated approval says nothing about the query, and one episode cannot establish a rule.
questions.hint: Check which link the notes leave out.

options.misconception: imposes a straight order on an account the notes do not order

options.text: A single failure, since the same source passage produced complaints in two different renderings.
options.misconception: treats a recurring complaint as one failure rather than as a pattern

options.text: No account at all, since complaints about a phrase say nothing about how the phrase was rendered.
options.misconception: dismisses the notes as irrelevant to how the phrase was rendered

options.text: A loop, since each response to a complaint produced the complaint that prompted the next response.

questions.explanation: Each response produced the complaint that prompted the next, so the notes describe a loop rather than a sequence with a beginning. The recurring complaint is part of the pattern, not a reason to dismiss the notes.

options.misconception: mistakes a condition present in every non-query for one that produces it

options.text: That the check was necessary for a passage to escape a query, but not sufficient, since checked passages were queried too.

options.misconception: asserts a producing power from a pattern of co-occurrence

answer.exemplar: The note establishes that repetition accompanies approval without producing it, because some approved renderings were never repeated to anyone. A condition present in every success and in no failure of the condition is insufficient on its own, and the note is careful not to claim that repeating a rendering would secure an approval, since the records do not show what the client did in any particular case. What the note can support is a weak pattern worth recording for future reference, and nothing firmer than that.

questions.explanation: Repetition accompanies approval without producing it, because some approved renderings were never repeated. A condition present in every success and sufficient for none is weak, and the note supports nothing firmer.
questions.hint: Ask whether approvals ever occurred without repetition.

options.text: That one rendering is better, since a dialogue line can be settled only by testing both in print.
options.misconception: presumes a print test is the only way to judge a rendering

That the renderings should not be reused, because no reader feedback exists for either of them.
options.misconception: infers a rule about reuse from the absence of reader feedback

questions.explanation: Each rendering was accepted by the client it was written for, so each is acceptable on its own terms. Nothing in the notes ranks the two, since acceptance by two clients is not a comparison.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A feedback loop that a linear account cannot order
questions.learningObjective: Present a self-feeding set of notes as a loop
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that a glossary's entries provoked queries, the queries changed the glossary, and the changed glossary provoked further queries. Explain how the translator should present this.

answer.exemplar: The translator should present it as a loop, because each element produces the next and none can be shown to be the starting point from the notes alone. A linear presentation would have to nominate one of the three as the beginning, and that nomination would be an addition rather than a finding, since the notes record mutual production rather than a single direction. The translator can still describe the sequence of concrete events, provided each is given with its date, but the account of how the glossary and the queries relate to each other should be stated as a loop so that the mutual dependence is not lost.

questions.explanation: It should be presented as a loop, because each element produces the next and no starting point is established. A linear version would have to nominate a beginning, which is an addition rather than a finding.
questions.hint: Ask whether any one element can be shown to come first.

options.misconception: treats another edition's practice as confirming the first rule

options.text: The threshold must be wrong, since a rule that changes with page number cannot be a real rule.
options.misconception: dismisses a rule because its boundary seems implausible

options.text: The page number is an artefact of the pagination, and the notes do not show what actually changed at that point.
The threshold should be moved to the end of the first edition, since the boundary must fall somewhere in the volume.
options.misconception: picks a boundary by convenience rather than by evidence

questions.explanation: A boundary at a page number may be an artefact of pagination, and the notes say nothing about what changed there, so no threshold is shown. The second edition's uniform practice settles nothing.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The scope condition as part of a finding
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a note records the scope of an observed practice
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that a policy described as applying to all staff was actually applied to one department in this project. Explain why the note must record the scope.

answer.exemplar: The note must record the scope because the source statement and the practice in this project do not match, and a reader who takes the source at its word would expect a rule covering every department, when what the translator observed was one. Recording the scope keeps the finding about this project, which is what the evidence supports, and it also leaves open the possibility that the policy is applied more widely elsewhere, which the notes do not settle. A note that simply repeats the source's general wording would give the reader a wider claim than the translator's own observation can carry.

questions.explanation: The note must record the scope because the source's wording and the observed practice do not match, and the evidence supports this project only. Repeating the source's wording would overstate the observation.
questions.hint: Ask how a reader would read the note without a scope.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Several routes to the same visible outcome
questions.learningObjective: State what two approved renderings in different editions support
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that a chapter was rendered in a plain style for one edition and a period style for another, and both were approved. What can the notes support?

options.text: That the period style was preferred, since a more careful rendering usually wins approval more often.
options.misconception: ranks styles by which one seems more likely to win approval

options.text: That the plain style was preferred, since plain writing suits a wider readership.
options.misconception: ranks styles by a general principle about plain writing

options.text: That the two styles are equally good, since both were approved and approval settles quality.
options.misconception: treats approval as a quality judgement rather than a decision

options.text: That each style was acceptable for the edition it was written for, and the notes hold no ranking between them.

questions.explanation: Each style was approved for the edition it was written for, so each was acceptable on its own terms, and the notes give no basis for ranking them. Approval is a decision, not a verdict on quality.
questions.hint: Ask what the notes compare the two editions on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The scope condition as part of a finding
questions.learningObjective: Scope a practice that appears in only part of a work
questions.stem: A translator's note records that first names were kept in the original script throughout one chapter and transliterated throughout another. What should the translator do before applying the practice elsewhere?

options.text: Record the scope as those two chapters, so the practice is not read as a rule for the whole work.
Record the practice as the translator's habit, since the note describes what the translator normally does.
options.misconception: generalises a bounded practice into a habit of the translator

options.text: Check whether the two chapters are long, since length decides whether a practice counts as a rule.
options.misconception: believes a chapter's length settles whether a practice is a rule

options.text: Record only the chapter where transliteration was used, since that is the more useful practice to keep.
options.misconception: keeps the practice the translator prefers and drops the other

questions.explanation: The practice is recorded in two chapters and not in the rest, so the scope must be stated. Otherwise it reads as a rule for the whole work, which the note does not support.
questions.hint: Ask where in the work the practice actually appears.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Applying a finding where its condition is not met
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish two different practices from one rule in two forms
questions.stem: A translator's note says that the client's convention was to translate a unit of measure into local units. A new job uses a client whose convention is to keep the original unit and add a gloss. What should the translator conclude?

options.text: The new client's convention is the same rule stated in different words, since both handle units explicitly.
options.misconception: treats two different conventions as the same rule in different words

options.text: The note's rule rests on the first client's convention, and the second client's convention is a different practice.
The new client should be asked to change its convention, since one consistent practice is better for a publisher.
options.misconception: assumes one practice is better regardless of the client

options.text: The translator should follow whichever convention the previous job used, since consistency across projects serves the reader.
options.misconception: prefers past consistency over the client's own convention

questions.explanation: The rule rests on the first client's convention, and the second client's practice is a different one, not a rewording. Consistency across projects is a preference, and this client has stated a convention.
questions.hint: Ask whose convention the note records.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why an order of events does not identify a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Explain the limit of a dated sequence for a claim about cause
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that the glossary was circulated, the client replied, the glossary was revised, and the revised glossary went to the typesetter. Explain what the notes can support about the cause of the revision.

answer.exemplar: The notes can support that the revision came after the client's reply and that the revised glossary is the one the typesetter received, because both are matters of order that the record fixes. They cannot support that the reply caused the revision, since the notes do not say what the reply contained or that the revision answered it, and a client who replies with general remarks can prompt a great many edits. The notes are careful on this point, and the translator should keep the claim in the same careful form rather than turning a sequence of dated steps into an explanation the file does not contain.

questions.explanation: The notes fix the order of the steps and the glossary the typesetter received, but not that the reply caused the revision, since the reply's content is unrecorded. Dated steps are not an explanation.
questions.hint: Ask what the reply actually said before crediting it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A feedback loop that a linear account cannot order
questions.learningObjective: Identify a loop that an earlier entry confirms

stimulus.body: A translator's notes record that a draft was sent to a reader, the reader's notes were returned, the draft was revised, and the reader's notes on the revision asked for further changes. An earlier entry in the same notes records that the reader had also asked for changes on a different draft before this exchange began.

questions.stem: Given these notes, which reading best fits the exchange they record?

options.text: A sequence, since the first draft and the first reply come before everything that follows.
options.misconception: orders a self-feeding exchange by the calendar alone

options.text: A single revision, since the notes describe one round of comments and one response to them.
options.misconception: collapses a repeating exchange into a single round of comments

options.text: A loop, since each round of comments produces the next, and the earlier entry shows the pattern predates the exchange.
An accident, since a reader asking for changes twice is unusual enough to need no explanation.
options.misconception: treats a recurring pattern as a curiosity needing no account

questions.explanation: Each round of comments produces the next, and the earlier entry shows the pattern was already running, so no round can be named first. The earlier entry is what rules out a single round of comments.
questions.hint: Ask what the earlier entry contributes to the reading.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Recognising and testing a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Judge how far a note about a boundary reaches
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that quoted passages up to a certain length were kept as quotations and longer ones were absorbed into the text. Which statement is best supported?

options.text: The threshold is at exactly sixty words, since quotations in the source are usually about that length.
options.misconception: invents a precise figure that the notes never give

options.text: The threshold is confirmed, because the notes describe what happened on both sides of it.
options.misconception: claims the notes bracket the change when they do not

options.text: There is no threshold, because a translator's decision about a quotation is always a matter of taste.
options.misconception: dismisses a recorded practice as pure taste

options.text: A boundary of some kind is recorded, but the notes do not fix where it lies.

questions.explanation: The notes record a change across a boundary, and without the longest kept quotation and the shortest absorbed one it cannot be placed. A figure and an appeal to taste are not in them.
questions.hint: Ask what two lengths would be needed to place the boundary.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Telling a necessary condition from a sufficient one
questions.learningObjective: Conclude correctly about a necessary but insufficient condition
questions.stem: A translator's note says that every rendering the client accepted had been checked for consistency of tense, and that many tense-checked renderings were sent back. What should the translator conclude and do?

options.text: Conclude that the tense check was needed for acceptance here but did not produce it, and record it in those terms.
Conclude that the tense check produced the acceptances, since every accepted rendering had passed it.
options.misconception: mistakes a condition in every acceptance for one that produced it

options.text: Conclude that the tense check was irrelevant, because some renderings were sent back after it.
options.misconception: treats a condition present in some failures as making it irrelevant

options.text: Conclude that the tense check was sufficient, since no rendering that passed it was accepted.
options.misconception: confuses a necessary condition with a sufficient one

questions.explanation: Every accepted rendering passed the tense check and many that passed were sent back, so the check was needed for acceptance without producing it. Sending them back shows the check was not enough.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to renderings that passed the check.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A condition present in every success and sufficient for none
questions.learningObjective: Classify a condition present in every approval
questions.stem: In a translator's notes, every rendering the client read aloud was approved, and many renderings the client did not read aloud were also approved. What follows about reading aloud?

options.text: Reading aloud produced the approvals, because every approved rendering was read aloud before delivery.
options.misconception: confuses a condition in every approval with one that produces it

options.text: Reading aloud is present in every approval but guarantees none, so it is a condition of little weight.
Reading aloud had no bearing on approval, since the notes record approvals rather than causes.
options.misconception: dismisses a condition because the notes were written to record approvals

options.text: Reading aloud was required for approval, since no approved rendering went unread aloud.
options.misconception: reads a merely sufficient condition as a necessary one

questions.explanation: Every approval came with the rendering read aloud, but plenty of unaloud ones were approved too. So the practice accompanies approval without producing it, and calling it necessary misdescribes it.
questions.hint: Ask whether unaloud renderings were ever approved.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Several routes to the same visible outcome
questions.learningObjective: Explain what several deliverable renderings establish
questions.stem: A translator's notes record that a line was rendered in three ways, and that all three were sent out and none was rejected. Explain what this can and cannot tell the translator.

answer.exemplar: The notes can tell the translator that more than one rendering of that line was considered deliverable, which is a useful fact when a later revision is needed and the earlier drafts are unavailable, since it shows the passage is not locked into a single form. The notes cannot tell the translator which of the three a reader would prefer, because no reader response is recorded, and they cannot tell the translator that the three are equivalent, because acceptance by a client is a decision about fitness for a purpose and not a measurement of quality. The honest use of the record is to widen the set of available routes and to say plainly that the notes do not rank them.

questions.explanation: The notes show that more than one rendering of the line was deliverable, which widens the options later. They cannot say which a reader would prefer, since no response is recorded, and acceptance is not a measure of quality.
questions.hint: Ask what the notes record beyond the fact of delivery.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The scope condition as part of a finding
questions.learningObjective: Describe a change in treatment and separate it from its cause

stimulus.body: A translator's notes record that in the work being translated, a term appears in the source language throughout the first three chapters and is translated from the fourth onwards. A separate line notes that the change coincides with the arrival of a new editor, and the notes do not say whether the editor instructed it.

questions.stem: Given these notes, what is the best description of the term's treatment?

options.text: The change was instructed by the new editor, since the change and the arrival of the editor coincide.
options.misconception: reads coincidence in timing as an instruction that was given

options.text: The treatment is inconsistent, so the notes give no finding about the term at all.
options.misconception: treats variation within a work as the absence of a finding

options.text: The treatment changes at a point in the work, and the notes record the change without recording its cause.
The term should be translated throughout, since consistency within a work is the usual requirement.
options.misconception: substitutes a general preference for what the notes record

questions.explanation: The notes record a change in treatment at a point in the work, and the coincidence with the editor's arrival is a timing fact, not a recorded instruction. Variation within a work is still a finding about that work.
questions.hint: Ask whether the notes record an instruction.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Applying a finding where its condition is not met
questions.learningObjective: Weigh a preference note against a new setting
questions.stem: A translator's note says the client preferred short chapters. A colleague proposes using that note to justify splitting chapters in a new translation for a different publisher. What is the strongest objection?

options.text: The colleague should ask the new publisher to confirm the preference, since preferences are always worth confirming.
options.misconception: asks for confirmation without identifying the condition at issue

options.text: Chapter length is a matter of layout rather than of translation, so the note should not be used at all.
options.misconception: dismisses the note as irrelevant on grounds of layout

options.text: Short chapters are less likely to be accepted than long ones, so the note is of doubtful value even in its own project.
options.misconception: judges a recorded preference by its worth rather than by its scope

options.text: The note's condition was one client's preference, and the new publisher's preference is a separate matter to establish.

questions.explanation: The note's condition was one client's preference, and the new publisher's must be established separately, so the note cannot be carried across. The note's worth in its own project is not the question.
questions.hint: Ask whose preference the note records.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Why an order of events does not identify a mechanism
questions.learningObjective: Set up the work needed before reading a record of steps
questions.stem: A translator's notes record: a source was received, a first draft was written, a reader commented, and a final draft went out. What should the translator do before drawing any conclusion about the process?

options.text: Establish what each step responded to, because the order alone does not say what produced what.
Arrange the steps in the order the translation industry usually works, so the record reads as a standard one.
options.misconception: reshapes the record to fit a standard picture of the process

options.text: Remove the reader's comment, since outside judgements do not belong in a translator's own record.
options.misconception: removes a step because it came from someone outside the translator

options.text: Give the reason for each step, since the reasons are obvious from the order and need no checking.
options.misconception: supplies missing explanations as though the record had made them

questions.explanation: The translator must establish what each step responded to, because the list fixes the order and nothing more. Arranging it to fit a standard picture, or supplying reasons, adds to the record.
questions.hint: Ask what each recorded step was a response to.
